full_title: BOHOL WISDOM SCHOOL, DR. SIMPLICIO YAP, JR., AND RAUL H. DELOSO, PETITIONERS, VS. MIRAFLOR MABAO, RESPONDENT.
subject: Labor Law and Social Legislation
syllabus_topic: VI. Suspension and Termination of Employment > A. Termination or Suspension by Employer > 2. Just Causes (DO 147, s. 2015)
topics: Immorality as a ground for discipline is judged by public and secular morality, not religious morality
Premarital sex and pregnancy out of wedlock between persons with no impediment to marry is not immoral
Suspension requires substantive and procedural due process; no substantial compliance when the penalty was decided before hearing the employee
Abandonment: unjustified absence plus overt act showing intent to sever the relationship

other_subjects.subject: Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics
other_subjects.syllabus_topic: III. Civil Procedure > S. Post-judgment Remedies > 5. Appeal and Review > e. Modes > v. Appeal by Certiorari to SC (Rule 45)

doctrine:
**Whether an employee's conduct is disgraceful or immoral is judged by public and secular morality, not religious morality.** Reiterating Leus v. St. Scholastica's College Westgrove and Inocente v. St. Vincent Foundation, the Court held that **sexual relations between two consenting adults with no legal impediment to marry, even if they result in pregnancy out of wedlock, are not disgraceful or immoral.** No law proscribes them, and they contravene no fundamental state policy in the Constitution. A sectarian school therefore cannot validly suspend a teacher for "immorality" because she became pregnant by her boyfriend before marriage, even if the conduct violates the school's religious standards. Such a suspension is illegal.

A suspension must also satisfy due process. It must rest on a just or authorized cause under the Labor Code, and the employee must be given notice and an opportunity to be heard before the penalty is decided. There is no "substantial compliance" where no notice to explain was issued and the employer had decided the penalty before hearing the employee.

Abandonment requires (1) failure to report for work or absence without valid or justifiable reason, and (2) a clear intention to sever the employer-employee relationship shown by an overt act. An employee who refuses return-to-work notices after her suspension ends and writes that she "could no longer go back to work for the school" abandons her employment as of that letter, and her money claims accrue only up to that date.
facts:
Miraflor Mabao had been a grade school teacher at Bohol Wisdom School (BWS) since June 7, 2007 and became regular in 2010. In September 2016 she told the principal and Raul Deloso, head of the Administrative Team, that she was two months pregnant by her boyfriend. Minutes of the Administrative Team meeting on September 21, 2016 showed that, before Mabao was brought into the meeting, the team had already decided to suspend her from September 22, 2016 until she was legally married. On September 22 she was verbally suspended. On September 27 she received a Disciplinary Form imposing "Indefinite suspension until legally married" and a Letter. The Letter cited RA 9710 ("The Magna Carta for Women") but held that premarital sex was immoral and that, as a grade school teacher, she was expected to have the highest moral standards. No written notice to explain was issued.

On October 5, 2016, Mabao married her boyfriend and filed a complaint for illegal suspension, illegal dismissal, separation pay, money claims, damages, and a certificate of employment. BWS sent three return-to-work notices, dated October 7, November 3, and November 22, 2016. Mabao refused to receive them, but she received the first by registered mail on October 24, 2016. In a letter dated November 9, 2016, she replied that the matter was already before the NLRC and that "I could no longer go back to work for the school." Her position paper prayed for separation pay in lieu of reinstatement because of strained relations.

The Labor Arbiter (January 31, 2017) found constructive dismissal and awarded backwages, separation pay, and benefits. The NLRC (May 31, 2017) reversed, finding no constructive dismissal. On certiorari, the CA (September 28, 2018 Decision; January 24, 2020 Resolution, CA-G.R. SP No. 11224) agreed that there was no constructive dismissal but held the suspension illegal. It awarded backwages from September 22 to October 7, 2016, 13th month pay and benefits until November 25, 2016, 10% attorney's fees, and a certificate of employment. BWS, Dr. Simplicio Yap, Jr. (Board Chairman), and Deloso filed a Rule 45 petition. They argued that the suspension was a valid exercise of management prerogative under the school's Christian standard of morality, and that due process was substantially complied with because Mabao was heard, admitted the violation, and agreed to the suspension.
issues: Whether the Court may review the factual findings in this Rule 45 petition.
Whether Mabao abandoned her employment, and when her employment ended.
ruling:
**1. Yes.** Only questions of law may be raised under Rule 45, but the Court may review the facts when the findings of the lower tribunals are inconsistent on material points, as they were here among the LA, the NLRC, and the CA.

**2. Yes, the suspension was illegal, both substantively and procedurally.** The standard of morality the law applies is "public and secular, not religious," and refers to conduct proscribed because it is detrimental to the conditions on which the existence and progress of human society depend. If government relied on religious beliefs to set public morals, it would require conformity to a religious agenda. Following Leus and Inocente, **sexual intercourse between two consenting adults with no legal impediment to marry, like Mabao and her boyfriend, is not immoral.** No law proscribes it, and it does not contravene any fundamental state policy. Mabao's premarital relations and resulting pregnancy were "not disgraceful or immoral within the contemplation of the law," so her suspension had no valid basis. The Court quoted with approval the CA's statement that "[o]n a secular level, premarital sex is not immoral per se."

The suspension also violated procedural due process. A suspension is reasonable only if it is based on just or authorized causes and the employee is given notice and an opportunity to be heard before judgment. BWS admittedly issued no notice to explain. The September 21, 2016 minutes showed that the Administrative Team decided the penalty before hearing Mabao, so **there was no substantial compliance.**

**3. Yes, Mabao abandoned her work, but as of November 9, 2016, not November 25, 2016.** There was no dismissal. BWS intended to take Mabao back once she married. Her suspension ended upon her marriage on October 5, 2016, and she was then obliged to return without need of a return-to-work order, but she never did. She ignored three return-to-work notices. Her November 9, 2016 letter, stating that she "could no longer go back to work for the school," was **the overt act showing a clear intention to sever the employment.** Her complaint and position paper praying for separation pay, and her statement at the mandatory conference that she was no longer interested in working at BWS, confirmed this. Her benefits therefore accrue only until November 9, 2016. Legal interest of 6% per annum applies from finality.
disposition: The petition was DENIED. The CA Decision dated September 28, 2018 and Resolution dated January 24, 2020 in CA-G.R. SP No. 11224 were AFFIRMED with MODIFICATION. Mabao was declared illegally suspended. BWS, Dr. Yap, and Deloso were ordered to jointly and solidarily pay her backwages from September 22, 2016 to October 7, 2016; 13th month pay, unpaid rice allowance, laundry allowance, midyear bonus, and proportionate vacation/sick leave accruing until November 9, 2016; and attorney's fees of 10% of the total award. They were also ordered to issue her a certificate of employment. All monetary awards earn 6% legal interest per annum from finality until full payment, and the records were remanded to the Labor Arbiter for computation.

bar_questions.q: Ana, a single teacher in a Catholic high school, became pregnant by her boyfriend, who is also single. The school suspended her without pay "until she is legally married," citing its policy that premarital sex is immoral and that teachers in a religious school must model Christian values. Ana questions the suspension. The school invokes its management prerogative. Is the suspension valid?

alac.answer: No. The suspension is illegal because Ana's conduct is not immoral under the applicable standard.
alac.legal_basis: Whether conduct is disgraceful or immoral is judged by public and secular morality, not religious morality. Sexual relations between two consenting adults with no legal impediment to marry, resulting in pregnancy out of wedlock, are not immoral. No law proscribes them, and they contravene no fundamental state policy. A suspension based on such conduct has no just cause and is illegal. (Bohol Wisdom School v. Mabao, G.R. No. 252124, July 23, 2024, reiterating Leus v. St. Scholastica's College Westgrove)
alac.application: Ana and her boyfriend are both single and have no legal impediment to marry. Their relationship and Ana's pregnancy may run against the school's Catholic teachings, but that alone does not make them immoral under public and secular standards. Management prerogative cannot justify a penalty that has no just cause, so the school cannot use its religious standard to suspend her.
alac.conclusion: Ana's suspension is illegal, and she is entitled to backwages for the period of the suspension.

bar_questions.q: Assume instead that the school's handbook validly penalizes certain acts. When Bea, a teacher, disclosed a violation, the school's discipline committee met without her and decided to suspend her for 30 days. It then called her into the meeting, where she admitted the violation and said she would accept the suspension. The suspension was put in writing. No notice to explain was ever served. The school argues that it substantially complied with due process because Bea was heard, admitted the violation, and agreed to the penalty. Is the school correct?

alac.answer: No. There was no substantial compliance with procedural due process.
alac.legal_basis: A suspension must be based on a just or authorized cause, and the employee must be given notice and an opportunity to be heard before the penalty is decided. Any disciplinary action affecting employment must pass due process scrutiny in both its substantive and procedural aspects. Where no notice to explain was issued and the employer decided the sanction before hearing the employee, the employer cannot claim substantial compliance. (Bohol Wisdom School v. Mabao, G.R. No. 252124, July 23, 2024)
alac.application: The committee fixed Bea's 30-day suspension before she was even brought into the meeting. Her later admission and acceptance came after the decision had been made, so she was not given a real chance to be heard before judgment. No notice to explain stated the charge and invited her written explanation. Putting the decision in writing does not cure the lack of prior notice and hearing.
alac.conclusion: The school did not substantially comply with procedural due process in suspending Bea.

bar_questions.q: Carla was suspended by her employer until a stated condition happened. The condition happened on March 1, after which the employer sent her three return-to-work notices, which she refused to receive. On March 20, she wrote the employer that, because of the humiliation she suffered, she "could no longer go back to work" for it. Her position paper before the Labor Arbiter prayed for separation pay in lieu of reinstatement. The employer never issued a termination letter. The CA held that Carla's employment ended on April 5, the deadline in the last return-to-work notice. (a) Did Carla abandon her work? (b) Until what date do her 13th month pay and other benefits accrue?

alac.answer: (a) Yes, Carla abandoned her work. (b) Her benefits accrue only until March 20, the date of her letter, not April 5.
alac.legal_basis: Abandonment requires (1) failure to report for work or absence without valid or justifiable reason, and (2) a clear intention to sever the employer-employee relationship manifested by an overt act. An employee's letter stating that she could no longer go back to work, together with her refusal of return-to-work notices and her prayer for separation pay, shows that intention, and the employment ends on the date of that overt act. (Bohol Wisdom School v. Mabao, G.R. No. 252124, July 23, 2024)
alac.application: Carla's suspension ended on March 1, after which she was obliged to return to work, yet she refused three return-to-work notices without valid reason. Her March 20 letter is the overt act showing her clear intention to end the relationship, and her prayer for separation pay confirms it. In Mabao, the Court rejected the CA's use of the deadline in the last notice and fixed the end of employment on the date of the employee's letter.
alac.conclusion: Carla abandoned her work as of March 20, and her benefits accrue only up to that date.

notes: The Court found abandonment even though the employee had filed a complaint for illegal suspension and illegal dismissal. It relied on her November 9, 2016 letter, her prayer for separation pay, her statement at the mandatory conference, and her refusal of three return-to-work notices. The LA's fallo gives the total award in words as ending "& 38/100" but in figures as PHP 320,678.19; the amount is omitted here because the LA decision was reversed. The fallo's "jointly and solidarity" is read as "jointly and solidarily."
